# Netplane

> Transport-independent Rust library for dynamically reconfigurable Tower service compositions.
> Generated by scripts/generate-llms-txt.sh. Version: 0.0.0

## Implemented

- Bounded Tower service execution with readiness and dispatch on the same service instance.
- Atomic publication of complete, immutable versions using ArcSwapOption.
- Synchronous version selection at Handle::execute() invocation; accepted requests retain that version until completion or future drop.
- Global synchronous admission limit across handles and versions, including unpolled futures.
- Queued-request cancellation, worker cleanup, and graceful, retryable shutdown draining.
- GraphBuilder's validated single-router composition over named Tower services and middleware.
- ReconfigurationController publication, rollback history, and structured runtime tracing.
- Optional netplane-http adapter with bounded body ingress and live listener reconfiguration.
- Optional netplane-control typed desired-state reconciliation with single-flight preparation and explicit publication conflicts.
- Optional netplane-kubernetes namespace-scoped Service and EndpointSlice discovery with immutable snapshots.
- Optional per-instance backend health, passive Tower observations, bounded active probes, and health-aware routing without graph republication.

## Limits and planned work

- Concurrency and buffer bounds are per version; the global admission budget bounds accepted, unfinished requests.
- GraphDraft validates positive capacities, not topology or application policy.
- GraphBuilder supports one validated router; arbitrary graph topology and application policy validation remain future work.
- HTTP ingress bounds begin after request headers are parsed. Encoded response size is checked after encoding.

- [crates/netplane](crates/netplane/): Public runtime library; transport and deployment independent.
- [crates/netplane-http](crates/netplane-http/): Optional HTTP adapter; depends on the core runtime.

# Netplane

The optional `netplane-http` workspace crate serves buffered HTTP requests through a Netplane handle. It bounds body size, body read concurrency, and read time, then rejects oversized encoded responses. See [HTTP resource boundaries](docs/http-boundaries.md) and `crates/netplane-http/examples/reconfigure.rs` for a persistent listener with process-local graph publication.

The [policy routing gateway](crates/netplane-http/examples/policy_gateway/README.md) is a persistent HTTP example with deterministic stable/canary routing, bounded execution, and graceful shutdown.

Netplane is an early stage Rust library for constructing and managing dynamically reconfigurable Tower service graphs. It aims to make graph publication, request lifetime, readiness, backpressure, and cancellation behavior explicit.

The repository provides bounded Tower service endpoints, a validated single-router `GraphBuilder`, conditional publication and rollback through `ReconfigurationController`, atomic publication of validated execution versions, graceful shutdown, and development tooling. Accepted requests retain the version selected at invocation. Successful shutdown releases the active graph, even when handles remain. Version `0.0.0` marks this pre-release stage; neither library crate is published.

## Scope

Netplane builds on `tower::Service`. The core is transport independent and testable with in-memory services. The optional HTTP adapter has its own crate; deployment integrations can be added behind real dependency boundaries. Netplane is not a standalone HTTP proxy or a replacement async runtime.

The design contract is in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md), with decisions recorded in [docs/adr](docs/adr). They distinguish current behavior from future requirements.

The [performance guide](docs/performance.md) describes the core benchmark suite, its Tower comparisons, and how to reproduce the [measured baseline](docs/performance-baseline.md). The [API review](docs/api-readiness.md) and [release checklist](docs/release-readiness.md) track work remaining before any publication decision.

## Get started

The repository pins Rust 1.88 in `rust-toolchain.toml`. See [QUICKSTART.md](QUICKSTART.md) for setup and verification commands.

```bash
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo run -p netplane --example live_reconfiguration
cargo run -p netplane --example controlled_reconfiguration
```

The workspace contains `crates/netplane` (the public library), `crates/netplane-http` (the optional HTTP adapter), and `crates/xtask` (development tooling). Dependencies are added only when used. `Cargo.lock` is ignored for this library workspace.

## Contribute

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before changing the architecture or public API. Report vulnerabilities through [the security policy](SECURITY.md). Netplane is licensed under [MIT](LICENSE).

## Weighted sticky routing

`WeightedRouting` is a transport-independent, immutable selector. Validate it
before building a graph and register its labels as routes:

```rust
use netplane::{GraphBuilder, WeightedRouting};
use std::convert::Infallible;
use tower::service_fn;

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync>> {
    let policy = WeightedRouting::try_new([("canary", 25), ("stable", 75)])?;
    let selector = policy.clone();
    let mut builder = GraphBuilder::new()
        .service("canary", service_fn(|_: String| async { Ok::<_, Infallible>("canary") }))
        .service("stable", service_fn(|_: String| async { Ok::<_, Infallible>("stable") }))
        .router("policy", move |key: &String| selector.select(key.as_bytes()).to_owned());
    for target in policy.targets() {
        builder = builder.route("policy", target, target);
    }
    let graph = builder.fallback("policy", "stable").entry("policy").validate()?;
    drop(graph);
    Ok(())
}
```

Names must be nonempty and unique; integer weights must sum to 100. Zero-weight
labels remain available for route registration. Selection accepts arbitrary key
bytes; HTTP key validation stays in the HTTP adapter or application.

The policy hashes keys using 64-bit FNV-1a modulo 100 and assigns cumulative
bucket ranges in configured order. Identical keys and policies repeat their
assignment. Increasing the first target's weight expands its range; other weight
or order changes may reassign keys. Percentages allocate sticky-key buckets,
not exact per-request traffic. FNV-1a is non-cryptographic and must not define an
authorization or security boundary.

Publish a replacement graph to change weights. Accepted requests retain the
policy from the version selected at `execute()` invocation, even when selection
runs later. Controller rollback restores the retained policy. The policy owns no
workers and performs no I/O. Selection itself allocates nothing; the current
router API requires the owned label shown above. Compare both costs with
`cargo bench -p netplane --bench routing -- routing/weighted`.

# Netplane agent coding contract

Netplane is a reusable Rust library with bounded Tower execution, immutable graph-version publication, request-version retention, and graceful shutdown. Read [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md), the [execution contract](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md), and the decisions in `docs/adr/` before changing the public API.

## Workspace

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/netplane` | Public, transport-independent runtime library. |
| `crates/netplane-http` | Optional bounded HTTP adapter and Axum listener integration; depends on the core. |
| `crates/xtask` | Development automation; never a runtime dependency of the library. |
| `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/adr/` | Design requirements and accepted decisions. |

Add crates only when a concrete dependency boundary emerges. Keep transport and deployment adapters outside the core. Add dependencies when they have consumers, use workspace versions, and minimize dependencies exposed by the public API.

## Netplane runtime invariants

- Preserve Tower readiness and dispatch on the same service instance and selected version, including across publication.
- Publish complete immutable versions atomically. Accepted requests retain their selected version and worker resources until completion or future drop.
- Preserve queued-request cancellation, worker cleanup, immediate shutdown admission closure, and retryable draining after a timeout. Dispatched cancellation depends on the service.
- Keep `crates/netplane` independent of transports and deployment systems.
- Preserve per-version concurrency and buffer bounds. A positive global admission budget bounds accepted, unfinished requests across versions and handles, including unpolled futures.
- `GraphDraft` validates positive capacities for a Tower service root. `GraphBuilder` validates its supported single-router topology, named backends, routes, fallback, and capacities. Neither validates application policy. Arbitrary DAGs, nested graphs, and dynamic node editing are unsupported.
- `ReconfigurationController` provides conditional publication, bounded rollback history, and inspection. Rollback republishes retained executable state under a new version ID.

## Design rules

- Interoperate with `tower::Service` and preserve readiness semantics. Avoid a competing service abstraction without a demonstrated need.
- Keep readiness and dispatch for each request on the same service instance and graph version, including across publication.
- Validate a replacement version before publishing it. Treat published versions as immutable.
- Make ownership and request lifetime explicit so in-flight requests keep required resources through completion or cancellation.
- Bound concurrency, queues, and task creation. Never hide overload with unbounded spawning.
- Keep locks out of `.await` spans. Use `tokio` only when runtime work needs it; offload blocking or long CPU work appropriately.
- Make cancellation, timeout, and shutdown cleanup observable and testable.
- Test core behavior with mock services, without sockets. Cover version lifetime, readiness, backpressure, concurrency, cancellation, and shutdown when changing those behaviors.
- Keep the implemented HTTP adapter and future deployment adapters outside the core runtime.

## Rust and API conventions

- Rust 2024, MSRV 1.88. Do not raise the MSRV without a dependency or feature requirement.
- Forbid unsafe code in the library. Use typed errors when needed; avoid `unwrap` and `expect` in production library code.
- Document every public item, including error and cancellation behavior. Prefer a small stable surface; keep implementation details private.
- Add or update meaningful tests before changing behavior. Inspect snapshot diffs before accepting them.
- Follow workspace lint settings. A justified lint exception belongs in the crate manifest with its reason.
- Keep source files under 500 lines. Do not put secrets or personal contact data in source or docs.
- `VERSION` and workspace version remain `0.0.0` until a deliberate release decision. The library is not currently published.

## Workflow

1. Check `git status`, nearby code, the architecture documents, and the current `.github/workflows/ci.yml` before editing.
2. Identify affected behavior and tests. Add tests first when changing logic.
3. Run focused checks. Use `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` when its optional tools are installed and its repository scan can run in the local environment. At minimum, run format, Clippy, build, and tests for code changes.
4. Update documentation when architecture or public behavior changes. Run `bash scripts/generate-llms-txt.sh` after significant architecture changes.
5. Use lowercase Conventional Commit subjects if asked to commit.

Use `rg` for repository searches and exclude `.git` and `target`. Repository skills in `.agents/skills/` contain detailed procedures, but this file is the project contract.

# Contributing to Netplane

Netplane is an early stage Rust library with bounded Tower execution, atomic version publication, cancellation, and graceful shutdown. `GraphBuilder` supports one router over named, independently bounded backends; arbitrary DAGs, nested graphs, and dynamic node editing are unsupported. Before proposing a broader topology, read [the architecture](docs/architecture.md), [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md), and [ADRs](docs/adr/), and explain how the change preserves Tower readiness, bounded resources, request lifetime, and transport independence.

## Set up

Follow [QUICKSTART.md](QUICKSTART.md) for the pinned toolchain and local commands. The workspace contains the transport-independent runtime in `crates/netplane`, the optional adapter in `crates/netplane-http`, and development tooling in `crates/xtask`.

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
```

Run `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` before submitting when the required local tools are installed. Runtime changes need focused tests with in-memory Tower services.

## Changes and review

Open an [issue](https://github.com/janagor/netplane/issues) for a substantial API or architecture change, or submit a draft pull request with a small prototype. Keep changes focused and document ownership, cancellation, readiness, and error behavior for new public APIs. Changes to execution, lifecycle, or publication need appropriate tests for version selection and lifetime, concurrent publication, cancellation and resource cleanup, shutdown and worker teardown, Tower readiness, and bounded execution. Update the canonical [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md) whenever runtime behavior changes. Keep transport adapters separate from the core.

Use lowercase [Conventional Commit](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) subjects, such as `docs: establish netplane architecture`. Update documentation for changed behavior and record durable design decisions in `docs/adr/`. Pull requests should include the verification commands run and any relevant limitations.

Netplane remains at version `0.0.0`; both library crates have `publish = false`. Publishing and compatibility policy will be decided before the first usable release. Do not trigger a release as part of an ordinary contribution.

Report vulnerabilities privately through [the security policy](SECURITY.md), not a public issue.

## Source: docs/architecture.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# Netplane architecture

## Status and purpose

Netplane is a Rust library for dynamically reconfigurable Tower service compositions. The workspace has a bounded Tower endpoint, immutable version publication, shutdown admission control, and `xtask`. [Execution semantics](architecture/execution-semantics.md) is the canonical contract for implemented runtime behavior.

## Design constraints

1. **Tower interoperability.** Compose with `tower::Service` and preserve its readiness contract. Introduce a Netplane-specific abstraction only when a working prototype shows why it is needed.
2. **Graph composition.** Use the implemented single-router `GraphBuilder` for named backend composition and ordinary Tower layers for middleware. Broader graph representations require a concrete use case.
3. **Immutable publication.** Build and validate a replacement configuration before publishing it. Active graph versions must not be modified in place.
4. **Request lifetime.** An in-flight request must retain the graph version and resources it needs until completion or cancellation. Readiness and dispatch for an individual request must operate on a consistent service instance and graph version. Graph replacement must not invalidate an outstanding readiness decision or prematurely release resources required by pending requests.
5. **Backpressure.** Bound concurrency and queues. Do not bypass readiness or spawn unbounded tasks to hide load.
6. **Cancellation and shutdown.** Define ownership and cleanup so cancellation, timeouts, and shutdown release resources without disrupting unrelated requests.
7. **Transport independence.** Core graph execution must be testable without sockets and must not depend on Hyper, Kubernetes, or a specific deployment system.
8. **Observability.** Instrument lifecycle and failures with `tracing` when the corresponding runtime behavior exists, without leaking sensitive request data.

## Workspace boundaries

| Path | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/netplane` | Public, transport-independent runtime library. Keep its public dependency surface small. |
| `crates/netplane-http` | Optional bounded HTTP ingress, outbound forwarding and Axum listener integration; depends on `netplane`. |
| `crates/netplane-control` | Optional typed desired-state reconciliation; depends on `netplane`. |
| `crates/netplane-kubernetes` | Optional namespace-scoped discovery and explicit endpoint translation; depends on runtime, control and HTTP adapters. |
| `crates/xtask` | Build and quality automation. Never a runtime dependency of `netplane`. |
| `docs/adr` | Accepted architectural decisions and their consequences. |

The HTTP adapter is a separate crate because body buffering, status mapping, and listener integration require protocol dependencies. The core does not depend on it.

## Implemented runtime

The in-memory runtime accepts a Tower service root, bounds its concurrency and buffer per version, enforces a global accepted-request budget, and publishes validated immutable versions atomically. Requests retain the version selected when `Handle::execute()` is called. Cancellation, worker ownership, and graceful shutdown follow the [execution contract](architecture/execution-semantics.md). Integration tests exercise publication, readiness, resource lifetime, and shutdown without sockets. `GraphBuilder` exposes the [composition prototype](adr/0004-graph-composition.md) as a validated single-router composition over named, independently bounded backend endpoints. Ordinary Tower layers provide middleware.

`WeightedRouting` supplies an optional immutable selector over ordered named backends. It validates integer percentages totaling 100 and deterministically assigns sticky keys using FNV-1a modulo 100. Policies own no services or workers; applications register policy labels with ordinary `GraphBuilder` routes and publish replacement graphs to change weights. Graph validation remains responsible for service references. Weights allocate key buckets rather than guaranteeing request traffic, and the non-cryptographic hash provides no security boundary.

The optional `netplane-control` crate adds [typed desired-state reconciliation](control-plane.md): explicit single-flight preparation, generation-aware deduplication, conditional publication, and explicit conflicts. An optional caller-owned single worker coalesces a bounded latest-value input,
retries classified failures with capped backoff, and discards superseded candidates.
[Reconciliation status and audit events](control-plane-observability.md) expose
desired and applied revisions independently of runtime publication generations.
Execution remains unchanged. [Progressive rollouts](progressive-rollouts.md)
submit guarded desired weight updates through that same worker, requiring complete
publication-attributed evidence before each advance. They add no request-path work.

The optional [`netplane-kubernetes`](../crates/netplane-kubernetes/README.md) crate observes Services and EndpointSlices through caller-owned watchers. It publishes immutable, normalized topology snapshots after complete per-collection initialization and relisting. Discovery is eventually consistent across resource collections. An explicit `ServiceBinding`
opts one Service into translation. `translate` resolves a Service port to normalized
TCP destinations using actual EndpointSlice ports, filters readiness and termination,
and includes Service and known Pod UIDs in semantic identity. Slice names, resource
versions and unrelated metadata do not participate in desired-state equality.

`KubernetesIntegration` forwards healthy complete snapshots to the existing
`ReconciliationDriver` using one coherent local `DiscoveryObservation`; it adds no
publication mechanism or event task scheduler. Unhealthy and rejected observations
invalidate pending candidates. The controller retains the driver's freshness guard
through the atomic swap, so candidates withdrawn before that swap cannot publish.
A publication that completes before invalidation remains active. Recovery resubmits
the latest valid observation; preparation cleanup can finish after invalidation.
Observation delivery coalesces intermediate values. A disconnect and recovery missed
by the bridge at an unchanged topology revision does not invalidate its candidate.
The freeze guarantee begins when the bridge processes a degraded or rejected
observation, rather than when discovery produces one.
`HttpGraphPreparer` uses ordinary bounded `GraphBuilder` backends and the core
`UniformRouting` policy. FNV-1a modulo the ordered endpoint count supplies equal-weight
selection for any positive backend count using a caller-provided key. An authoritative
empty topology compiles to a bounded Tower root returning typed `Unavailable`, mapped
to HTTP 503. API recovery, partial relists and invalid candidates retain the active
graph. `publishNotReadyAddresses` is explicitly rejected.

HTTP clients and connection pools are version-local. Execution workers and queues
are never shared between versions. This safely isolates known Pod replacement at a
reused IP; a removed endpoint's old pool remains usable by accepted requests and
bounded rollback history. Idle pools expire after 30 seconds and retain at most eight
connections per destination. `UpstreamLimits::max_backends` bounds workers per
candidate; runtime-wide admission and each backend's concurrency/queue capacity still
apply. Applications must bound HTTP request bodies at ingress. No retry or Kubernetes API call occurs during request execution. Optional health
observations and separately budgeted active checks follow the
[health contract](architecture/health.md). Applications
cancel discovery and its integration alongside runtime shutdown and await their
caller-owned tasks, as shown in `discovered_gateway`. A retained graph cannot ensure
a physically terminated Pod remains reachable.

Health-aware routing composes live per-instance handles with immutable policy
membership. Passive Tower layers and optional bounded active probes update a shared
state machine without publication. See [backend health](architecture/health.md).

## Current limits and future work

A positive runtime admission limit bounds accepted, unfinished requests across all versions and handles; excess requests are rejected immediately. `GraphDraft` validates capacities only. `GraphBuilder` validates its declared single-router topology and capacities, but cannot prove application policy or selector behavior. Arbitrary directed graphs, cycles, shared nodes, and dynamic node editing require a concrete use case before implementation. Structured tracing events are documented in [Runtime observability](observability.md). `ReconfigurationController` provides conditional publication, bounded rollback history, and inspection. The optional HTTP adapter reads and decodes bounded bodies before selecting a version through `try_execute`.

## Decisions

- [ADR 0001: Tower service model](adr/0001-tower-service-model.md)
- [ADR 0002: Runtime reconfiguration](adr/0002-runtime-reconfiguration.md)
- [ADR 0003: Crate boundaries](adr/0003-crate-boundaries.md)
- [ADR 0004: Internal graph composition prototype](adr/0004-graph-composition.md)
- [ADR 0005: Reconfiguration control](adr/0005-reconfiguration-control.md)

Inherited tooling ADRs in `docs/adr/tooling/` are not Netplane runtime design decisions.

- [ADR 0006: Backend health](adr/0006-backend-health.md)

- [ADR 0007: Progressive rollouts](adr/0007-progressive-rollouts.md)

## Source: docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/architecture.

# Execution semantics

This is the canonical contract for the implemented runtime. `crates/netplane` executes a Tower service root; `GraphBuilder` compiles one supported router topology with a buffered default and optional backend-only routing. See also [routed-execution.md](routed-execution.md).

## Validation and publication

`GraphDraft` accepts a Tower service root, including one built with `ServiceBuilder` and layers. Its validation checks positive concurrency and buffer capacities and starts a Tower buffer worker. `GraphBuilder` accepts named Tower services, one request selector, declared route labels, an explicit fallback, and a router entry. Validation checks references, duplicate declarations, reachable backends, supported topology, and positive active outer, default backend, and explicit backend capacities before starting any workers. An explicit service capacity overrides the default regardless of builder call order; the declared default must still be valid. Metadata records the active outer capacity as `Some` for buffered graphs or `None` for backend-only graphs, plus the configured backend default and every backend's effective capacity in name order. Changing a capacity requires publishing a replacement graph version. Selector labels without a declared route use the fallback. Route and fallback declarations require a previously registered router; services and the entry can be declared in any order. The builder cannot prove application policy or interpret selector logic. The [live reconfiguration example](../../crates/netplane/examples/live_reconfiguration.rs) applies simulated authorization through ordinary Tower layers on each backend. That filter runs after route selection and backend readiness.

`Handle::execute()` admits a request and selects an immutable graph version synchronously when called, before its returned future is polled. Route selection is lazy: backend-only graphs run the selector on the first poll of the accepted future, and buffered graphs run it when the outer worker dequeues the request. Unpolled or already-expired futures therefore do not invoke the selector or submit to a backend. `Netplane::publish()` atomically replaces a complete version using `ArcSwapOption`. An accepted request keeps its selected version through completion or future drop, so an old request can finish after a new composition is published. The Tower buffer worker polls readiness and calls the same owned service instance. Requests selected after publication use the new version.

`ReconfigurationController` exclusively owns a `Netplane` publisher and serializes conditional publication and rollback. Callers obtain an inspection snapshot with a runtime-scoped `VersionToken`, build and validate a candidate based on that snapshot outside the controller lock, then submit both for publication. A foreign or stale token is rejected without changing the active graph. Each successful replacement or rollback receives a fresh, increasing `VersionId`. Rollback republishes a retained executable graph and shares its existing Tower services and state; it does not reconstruct or reset them. History contains the most recently displaced publications in publication order, up to `ControllerOptions::max_retained_versions` (two by default, zero to disable rollback). Eviction releases only controller references; selected request futures can still own older versions.

## Capacity and cancellation

`GraphDraft` versions use one Tower concurrency limit and bounded buffer. `GraphBuilder` versions give each named backend its own Tower concurrency limit and buffer, plus a bounded outer Tower endpoint and worker by default. `GraphBuilder::without_outer_capacity()` removes the outer endpoint and aggregate per-version execution limits while retaining backend limits and `RuntimeLimits::max_outstanding`. Explicit outer capacity conflicts with the opt-out in either call order. Capacity is not shared across retained versions; a transition can therefore have work executing in both versions. Callers waiting for outer or backend queue capacity remain pending. `RuntimeLimits::max_outstanding` bounds all accepted, unfinished request futures across versions and cloned handles, including unpolled futures and queue waiters. Admission happens synchronously at `Handle::execute()` or `try_execute()` invocation. At the limit, `try_execute()` returns `AdmissionError::AtCapacity` immediately; `execute()` returns a future containing that boxed error. Completion or future drop releases one slot. Publication does not reset the budget, and old-version requests keep their slots until completion or drop. Shutdown closure takes precedence over overload. This limit does not bound tasks spawned by services or request memory. The example routes requests between two independently bounded backend endpoints. Backend A initially withholds readiness while backend B remains ready, demonstrating independent backend progress when outer execution capacity is available. Its backend filters check a caller-provided Boolean after routing. Each selected backend endpoint polls readiness before dispatch. Backpressure appears while an execution future waits on a saturated backend; outer in-flight slots can also cause head-of-line blocking. Independent backend readiness does not guarantee progress for a ready branch if other requests occupy every outer slot. This is only a simulated authorization decision, not identity authentication.

Dropping a queued request cancels its wait. Dropping a dispatched request future releases its global admission slot, but cancellation of the underlying call depends on the service. Thus `max_outstanding` bounds accepted Netplane request futures, not all service executions that may continue after cancellation. Netplane owns each Tower buffer worker and aborts it when the last owning endpoint and request future reference disappears, including when the worker is stuck in readiness.

## Request ownership and deadlines

Each successful admission acquires exactly one global slot through an admission guard. The returned future owns that guard and the selected immutable publication until it completes or is dropped, including while unpolled, waiting for buffer capacity or readiness, and after dispatch. Completion, cancellation, and deadline expiration release the guard once. Publication cannot move an admitted request to a newer version. At most one active version plus versions retained by accepted requests, controller history, and external owners remain referenced by Netplane's publication and request state. This does not bound resources retained independently by services or candidate graphs built before publication.

`Handle::try_execute_until` and `Handle::execute_until` require a per-request absolute Tokio deadline. Callers choose the original methods when they do not want one. The deadline starts when the API is invoked, before first poll. Admission and version selection still happen synchronously. An already elapsed deadline is reported on first poll without polling the endpoint. An unpolled future continues to own its slot and version until polled or dropped; Netplane creates no timer task for it. An active expiration drops the Netplane execution future and returns a boxed `DeadlineExceeded`. A completion observed before the deadline returns normally. At the exact deadline, the initial expiration check takes precedence; after execution begins, Tokio's `timeout_at` resolves the race according to its polling behavior.

Expiration while waiting for queue capacity cancels the caller's wait. During service readiness, it cancels the caller's future but does not necessarily stop the shared Tower buffer worker from polling readiness for a queued request. The worker remains owned by the endpoint and can resume when readiness changes. After dispatch, the underlying service may keep work alive according to its own cancellation behavior. Timeout produces one `request.failed` terminal event with `error_kind = "deadline_exceeded"`; dropping a request future produces `request.cancelled`. Service failures and closed buffer workers remain separate failure categories. Worker termination wakes affected buffer callers with errors; Netplane does not restart or replay their requests. Shutdown closes new admission immediately, while already accepted requests continue under their own deadlines. A shutdown timeout changes only the drain attempt and never reopens admission.

## Shutdown

Calling `Netplane::shutdown(grace_period)` closes admission synchronously across handles, even before its returned future is polled. Publication is rejected from that point. Shutdown waits for accepted request futures to complete or be dropped, including futures never polled. A timeout reports the outstanding count and leaves admission closed and draining, so shutdown can be retried. A successful drain clears the active graph even if inactive handles remain. Shutdown cannot forcibly reclaim resources held by an uncooperative user-owned future or tasks spawned independently inside a service.

Calling `ReconfigurationController::shutdown` closes admission under its control mutex before returning the drain future, then clears controller history. Publication and rollback are rejected from that point, including after a timed-out drain. A later call retries the same runtime drain.

## Observability and adapter boundary

The runtime emits [structured tracing events](../observability.md) for admission, completion, cancellation, validation, publication, worker termination, and shutdown. Accepted-to-terminal duration includes any time before the first poll. A replaced version is released only after its last owner drops. The optional `netplane-http` adapter selects a version after bounded body collection and decoding. A disconnected client need not immediately drop its handler, and dispatched service work may survive handler cancellation.

`Handle::status()` returns a read-only `RuntimeStatus` sampled from one admission-state lock. Its count includes all accepted, unfinished Netplane futures across handles and versions; its lifecycle is `Running`, `Draining`, or `Stopped`. Calling shutdown enters `Draining` synchronously. Timeout leaves that phase in place, and only a successful drain enters `Stopped`. This sample and `ReconfigurationController::inspect()` are independent observations and need not reflect the same instant. Controller history length counts retained publication entries, not live executable graphs or services. The gateway's `/status` endpoint includes both views while its listener remains available.

`version.released` means a publication wrapper lost its last owner. A rollback can make two publication IDs share one executable graph, so this event alone does not prove that its Tower workers were destroyed. Arbitrary graph construction and policy validation remain future work.

For buffering, admission timing, response ownership, and listener shutdown at the HTTP boundary, see [HTTP resource boundaries](../http-boundaries.md).

## Health eligibility

Optional [backend health](health.md) is sampled when lazy route selection runs
inside the pinned graph. Selection failures dispatch no backend or fallback.
Once selected, a destination is retained across health changes, publication and
queue waits. Health updates never retry, reroute, or publish a graph.

## Source: docs/architecture/health.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/architecture.

# Backend health and eligibility

Health is optional operational state composed with ordinary Tower services and
existing routing policies. Discovery determines graph membership and readiness;
health only removes candidates from that membership. Health observations never
publish a graph, mutate configured weights, retry, or move dispatched requests.

## Identity and ownership

`HealthRegistry` registers a `BackendIdentity` containing service, instance, and
incarnation strings. Use a stable endpoint identity and a physical replacement
identifier, such as a Pod UID. Never identify every endpoint by service name alone.
Compatible repeated registrations share state. A different policy or recovery mode
for a still-live identity is rejected; it cannot reset a retained graph's state.
Replacing an incarnation creates independent state. An unknown incarnation cannot
be inferred from an IP address; applications must supply one when discovery cannot.

The registry indexes weak references. Handles in graph selectors, wrapped services,
probe registrations, and observation tokens retain records. Publication, rollback,
and candidate cleanup therefore follow ordinary ownership. Old graphs retain their
own membership and health handles. Final reference release reclaims the record.

## Recovery and observations

`HealthPolicy` uses nonzero consecutive failure and recovery thresholds and a
monotonic cooldown. Passive backends start healthy. Failure threshold exhaustion
marks a backend unhealthy. After cooldown it becomes recovering and can receive
ordinary weighted traffic to collect recovery evidence. This is not a circuit
breaker: there is no dedicated half-open request budget.

Active backends start recovering and remain ineligible until enough successful
active probes arrive. `begin_observation()` marks passive execution and
`begin_probe()` marks a probe; each token retains its source. Passive successes
never advance active-mode recovery, including calls selected earlier that begin
execution after cooldown. Those calls finish on their original backend. Valid
failures from either source return a recovering backend to unhealthy. Failed recovery returns to unhealthy and restarts cooldown.
Active and passive observations share the same state machine. Successful checks
while unhealthy cannot bypass cooldown. Cooldown transitions are advanced lazily
by observation or inspection; Tokio's monotonic clock supports deterministic tests.
Ignored observations change neither counters nor observation timestamps. Reporting
samples monotonic time after acquiring the per-record mutex, matching serialized
update order; observation timestamps and cooldown transitions cannot be backdated
by a reporter that waited for the lock.

Each execution captures an owning observation token at `Service::call`. Tokens
identify the record and health generation. State transitions invalidate earlier
tokens, preventing delayed successes from restoring a backend after exclusion.
A token cannot report against another incarnation. Counters saturate rather than
wrap. `HealthLayer` forwards readiness to the exact wrapped instance, preserves
result types, and records each completion once. Dropping its future records
nothing. Apply it directly to backend execution, inside Netplane's queues and
capacity limits, so local admission and saturation are never backend failures.
For deadlines, wrap an upstream execution timeout inside the health layer;
a deadline on the outer runtime future is caller cancellation, not evidence.

## Routing

`HealthAwareRouting` binds one health handle per `WeightedRouting` label. It samples
each positive-weight candidate once into a stack mask, then selects with the
existing FNV-1a hash modulo remaining total weight. Selection is O(N), allocates
nothing, and preserves existing bucket assignments when all candidates are
eligible. Weights remain immutable. `UniformRouting::select_eligible` supports
discovered endpoint sets; sets up to 128 use stack storage, larger sets use one
bounded-by-membership mask allocation.

An eligibility mask samples independent records sequentially, not a simultaneous
transaction across the registry. Once sampled, it is fixed for that routing
decision. Concurrent updates affect later decisions. Stronger cross-backend
snapshot consistency is not promised.

Use `GraphBuilder::try_router` to propagate `RoutingError::NoEligibleBackends`.
Errors dispatch no backend, including the declared fallback. Successful unknown
labels retain ordinary fallback behavior. Both buffered and backend-only graphs
use current health when route selection runs inside the pinned graph. A previously
selected destination remains fixed while waiting for its backend or executing.

Removing a stable backend can shift all selectable traffic to a canary, regardless
of configured canary percentage. Future rollout policies must inspect operational
eligibility as well as configured weights.

## Active checks

`HealthScheduler` is caller-owned; create it, obtain its registration handle, and
run its `run` future on Tokio. Configuration requires positive interval and timeout,
nonzero global concurrency, and an explicit maximum registration count. Hold each
`ProbeRegistration` alongside the graph or configuration that needs it. Unchanged
registrations share one check only when the health record and `ProbeIdentity`
configuration key both match. Incompatible probe configuration returns typed
`IncompatibleProbeConfiguration`; the old registration remains unchanged. A key
must cover all behavior-affecting settings. Probe configuration is distinct from
physical incarnation: do not change a backend incarnation to change a probe path.

The scheduler starts no permanent endpoint tasks. It keeps bounded registration
metadata and at most the global limit of check tasks. Each backend has at most one
running check. The next deadline follows completion; missed intervals do not queue.
Oldest due registrations run first. Probe timeouts report failure, registration
cancellation reports nothing, and shutdown aborts and joins managed checks.
`HealthSchedulerHandle::status()` exposes registered and running counts alongside
both configured limits. The registration budget covers the **union** of identities
held by active, historical, in-flight, and candidate graphs. It is not just an
active-topology limit. A full active topology needs replacement headroom: with a
budget of 100 and 100 active endpoints, replacing one requires 101 live identities
during preparation. Retrying cannot converge while every old lease remains held.
Retained history and unpolled admitted futures can prolong that requirement.
Capacity becomes available only after the last relevant lease drops; snapshots
help operators distinguish that condition from probe concurrency saturation.

Probe completion is accepted while holding the same registration mutex used by
removal. If acceptance wins, the health state update completes before removal can
return. If removal wins, the obsolete completion is discarded. Tracing callbacks
and final record destruction run after unlocking, so subscribers may inspect the
scheduler. Delaying callbacks cannot apply an old result to a replacement probe.

Checks consume an independent budget, never runtime admission. Shared HTTP client
pools still require sensible concurrency limits. Dropping `run` aborts managed
work; await shutdown completion when synchronous resource reclamation matters.

## Adapter boundaries

`netplane-http::health` supplies a configurable status classifier and a bounded
GET probe. Its compatibility identity includes origin, path, response bound,
classifier overrides and transport identity. An opaque caller-provided reqwest
client cannot be introspected: the default conservatively shares only upstream
clones. `with_transport_key` explicitly declares compatibility of separately built
clients; callers must include timeout, proxy, retry, redirect, protocol, and TLS
behavior in that key. Kubernetes supplies a key for its controlled client settings,
including exchange timeout. The passive default treats 2xx as success, 5xx as
failure, and other statuses as ignored. The active probe default requires 2xx and
treats all other statuses as failure; a missing or redirected health endpoint therefore fails the health
contract. Explicit overrides remain available through `with_classifier`.
Upstream transport errors and exchange timeouts fail; local runtime errors do not.
The HTTP error mapper maps no eligible backend to 503.

Kubernetes translation first filters readiness and termination. The optional
health configuration on `HttpGraphPreparer` reuses endpoint identities including
Service and known Pod UIDs. A healthy local record cannot re-add a discovery-excluded
endpoint. Readiness changes do not reset unchanged local state. Netplane writes no
Kubernetes resource to communicate local observations.

## Diagnostics and measurement

Registry snapshots expose owned per-backend state and aggregate counts. These are
diagnostic samples across records, not a global transaction. State transitions emit
structured tracing events after releasing state locks. Successful requests and
probes do not emit INFO events. Active check counts cover executing probe futures.

Run `cargo bench -p netplane --bench health` for disabled, all-healthy,
partially-unhealthy, concurrent-observation, and observation-update measurements.
The 128-label weighted fixture has 100 positive weights and 28 zero weights because
the existing integer percentage policy cannot express 128 positive targets.
Performance results depend on host and contention; a five-percent target is an
aspiration, not an API guarantee. See the [measured benchmark results](../health-performance.md).

## Source: docs/control-plane.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# Typed desired-state reconciliation

The optional `netplane-control` crate depends on `netplane`; the runtime does not
depend on it. It translates application configuration into conditional graph
publications through explicit `Reconciler::apply` calls or an optional caller-owned
`ReconciliationDriver`. It includes no file reader or discovery integration.

## Application contract

Implement `GraphPreparer<D, Request, Response>` and supply a shared
`Arc<ReconfigurationController<Request, Response>>` to `Reconciler::new`.
Desired state implements `Clone + Eq + Send + Sync`; the preparer is `Sync`.
Normalize configurations before submission so equality means equivalent policy.
The control crate imposes no universal configuration schema and does not compare
Tower service objects.

`validate(&desired)` checks application policy synchronously, before deduplication
or service construction. `prepare(desired)` asynchronously constructs services and
returns a validated `GraphVersion` using `GraphDraft` or `GraphBuilder`. Preparation
runs on the caller's executor outside the controller lock. Bound preparer resource
use and offload blocking work explicitly. Runtime graph validation still checks
capacities and supported topology; application policy belongs to the preparer.

## Publication and concurrency

Each reconciler admits one polled application at a time using a preparation permit.
A concurrent call returns `ApplyError::Busy`, without validation or preparation.
After validation, the reconciler inspects the active publication and its token.
If the last successful desired state compares equal and its publication is still
active, the result is `ApplyOutcome::Unchanged` with no construction or generation
change. This is a successful no-op at the observed publication generation, not a
guarantee of current convergence. Another publisher can replace that generation
before the caller receives the result.

Otherwise, the reconciler prepares one candidate and calls `publish_if_current`
with the original token. Success returns `ApplyOutcome::Applied` and records
`LastApplied { desired, published }` before any further await. `last_applied()`
returns a shared historical record; it does not claim that publication remains
active. Publication generations are distinct from application configuration revisions.
An external replacement or rollback invalidates deduplication even when the desired
configuration is equal, because rollback creates a fresh publication generation.

Validation and preparation errors preserve both the active graph and the last
successful record. Publication errors expose the existing `ControllerError`,
including `Stale` and `ShuttingDown`. Rejected candidates are dropped. Conflicts
never retry automatically: the caller decides whether explicit resubmission is
appropriate. Separate reconcilers have separate permits and can conflict through
the shared controller. Their last-applied records remain independent.

For integrations, prefer one authoritative reconciler per managed runtime, with
multiple configuration producers feeding it. Coordinate discovery, file updates,
and administrative changes through that owner to avoid competing sources
continually replacing each other. This is an integration recommendation, not an
API restriction; PR4 permits multiple reconcilers sharing a controller.

Dropping an application future during preparation drops its candidate resources
and releases its permit. Resources or tasks independently retained by an application
preparer remain its responsibility. There is no await between successful publication
and updating the local record. Accepted runtime requests keep their selected graph
through publication and can finish afterward. Shutdown visible at inspection rejects
before preparation; shutdown racing with preparation rejects at conditional publication.

## Example and verification

Run `cargo run -p netplane-control --example typed_reconciliation`. The example
applies A, accepts a request on A, publishes B, skips duplicate B, rejects invalid C,
and verifies that A completes while B remains active. Deterministic in-memory tests
also cover dispatched request lifetime, stale tokens, external replacements,
preparation failure, single-flight admission, candidate cleanup, and shutdown races.

## Bounded update driver

`ReconciliationDriver::new(reconciler, policy)` returns a worker and cloneable
`UpdateSender`. Construction spawns nothing; run `driver.run(is_transient)` on a
caller-owned executor, retaining its join handle. Producers call `submit(desired)`
to overwrite one latest-value slot. Each submission receives a checked, locally
increasing sequence independent of application revisions. Input retained during
startup, preparation, and backoff has constant slot count. Configuration sizes
and resources retained independently by applications remain application limits.

Only one preparation runs. A newer input does not cancel an active preparation;
the worker awaits completion and discards an obsolete candidate before conditional
publication. The last valid runtime graph remains available on failure.

`UpdateSender::invalidate_pending()` advances the shared sequence and withdraws
pending desired work without stopping the driver. It reports `Invalidated(sequence)`
through driver status and `Blocked` with failure `Invalidated` through reconciliation
status. It does not invent an applied revision or change the active graph. Recovery
requires a new submission, including when the desired state compares equal.

The final freshness check returns a mailbox read guard that the controller retains
through its atomic swap. Submissions, invalidation and driver shutdown acquire the
mailbox's write lock. If a swap wins first, its graph remains active; after invalidation
or shutdown returns, no earlier candidate can commit. This closes the former gap
between freshness checking and publication. Preparation and retry remain single-flight
and may finish before their withdrawn resources are dropped. Await the worker to
confirm cleanup. No mailbox guard or controller lock crosses an await, tracing
callback or displaced-resource cleanup; the lock order is mailbox then controller.

Defaults are a 100 ms quiet period, a one-second maximum coalescing window, and
exponential retry delays from 100 ms up to five seconds, with deterministic local
jitter of up to 20 percent of the capped exponential base, with fractional
nanoseconds truncated. The result is then clamped to at least one nanosecond and
at most the retry maximum; the five-second cap includes jitter. Zero debounce
bypasses the quiet period; other scheduling durations must be positive and ordered.
Continuous input cannot indefinitely postpone starting preparation, though a
candidate superseded during preparation is still discarded. Convergence assumes
updates eventually stabilize, preparation completes, and dependencies recover.

Validation failures are permanent. `run`'s classifier decides whether preparation
errors are transient. Stale publication tokens cause a fresh inspection and rebuild
after backoff; publication always remains conditional. Runtime shutdown exits the
worker; foreign-runtime and exhausted-generation failures wait for new input.
New input interrupts backoff and resets retry accounting. `max_retry_attempts`
counts retries after the initial attempt; `None` retries indefinitely. Exhausted
or permanent inputs remain in the latest slot and can be explicitly resubmitted.
After success, external publications require resubmission to detect drift.

Subscribe through `driver.status()` before moving the worker. This bounded watch
reports the latest preparation, success, typed failure and optional retry delay,
or graceful stop; it is not an audit stream. `UpdateSender::shutdown()` closes
input immediately. Await the worker to confirm cleanup: active preparation is
allowed to finish before the worker exits, so uncooperative preparation can delay
graceful shutdown indefinitely. Earlier candidates cannot commit after shutdown
returns, although a prior completed swap remains active. Dropping all producers also stops the worker. For forced
cancellation, drop the worker future, or abort and join its task. This drops
preparation according to the preparer's cancellation contract. There are no independently spawned worker tasks or retry timers.
Driver shutdown does not shut down the runtime or disrupt accepted requests.

Run `cargo run -p netplane-control --example burst_updates` for a complete producer,
status subscription, and joined shutdown example. Paused-time tests cover bursts,
superseded preparation, retry interruption and exhaustion, stale tokens, bounded
coalescing windows, and shutdown during preparation or retry.

Read [reconciliation observability](control-plane-observability.md) for consistent
desired/applied revision snapshots, bounded status subscriptions, and structured
audit events. The Kubernetes adapter uses coherent discovery observations and
invalidation to hold the active graph while discovery is unhealthy or invalid.

Progressive traffic policies use the [rollout contract](progressive-rollouts.md)
and reuse the same worker rather than publishing graphs independently.

## Source: docs/progressive-rollouts.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# Guarded progressive rollouts

`netplane_control::rollout` changes desired traffic policy through the existing
reconciliation worker. It does not execute requests, manage deployments, promote
instances, or automatically restore earlier traffic. The application supplies
`TrafficConfiguration` for its typed desired state and an `ObservationProvider`
for publication-attributed, backend-group-specific evidence. Core runtime status
and N10 health counts alone cannot establish canary success.

## Starting and owning a worker

First submit the baseline desired configuration through `UpdateSender` and await
convergence. Call `RolloutDriver::start(updates, provider, spec, poll_interval)` to
receive `(driver, handle)`, then poll `driver.run()` alongside the existing
`ReconciliationDriver::run()`. Construction spawns nothing. The application owns,
cancels and awaits both workers alongside runtime shutdown. Reconciliation worker
shutdown also terminates a paused or blocked rollout. Dropping the rollout future
cancels its observation and withdraws any owned uncommitted intent. Independently
spawned work inside application providers or preparers remains their responsibility.

One permit, shared by all producers of a reconciler, permits at most one pending,
active, paused or blocked rollout. Terminal completion or worker drop releases it.
Status is a bounded watch snapshot; intermediate transitions may coalesce.

`TrafficConfiguration::group_policy` resolves logical stable and canary groups,
which may contain many discovered endpoints. The two group weights must sum to
100. `set_weights` changes only those groups and must preserve unrelated desired
state. The preparer remains responsible for compiling those weights into existing
`WeightedRouting` or `HealthAwareRouting` and validating application policy.
`membership_revision` identifies material membership changes, including replacement
of an endpoint at a reused address. This identity is supplied by the integration.

## Specification and evaluation

`RolloutSpec` owns distinct group names and a nonempty stage sequence ending at
100% canary. Integer percentages are checked in 0..=100 and cannot decrease.
The first stage must not be below the currently applied canary allocation.
Every stage has explicit conditions and a finite positive observation deadline
strictly longer than its minimum observation duration. A 0% preflight stage may
check eligibility but cannot require canary traffic. Every positive canary stage
must require positive canary samples. Stable traffic conditions are invalid at
100% canary. No timing, error-rate, latency or sample thresholds are library defaults.

Conditions use AND semantics. Error-rate thresholds are exact integer basis
points in 0..=10,000; comparison uses widened integer products, without rounding
or floating point. Statistical conditions carry their own positive minimum sample
count. A definite violation takes precedence over another condition's missing
evidence. Eligibility is an explicit nonstatistical condition and may fail
immediately. The minimum duration gates success; elapsed time never replaces
samples. The final 100% stage must independently pass before completion.

The evaluator rejects incomplete windows, duplicate or missing groups, failure
counts above completed counts, mismatched publications, and mismatched epochs.
Missing latency, zero actual canary requests and source unavailability cannot pass.
A provider operation is bounded by both the polling interval and stage deadline.
Provider calls remain at least one polling interval apart across eligibility and
configuration restarts. Lifecycle and reconciliation changes interrupt waits to
revalidate or cancel work, but do not move the next provider-call deadline earlier.
Timeout and lost ownership remain halted until explicit resume, even if unrelated
configuration or membership updates subsequently converge. Pending compatible
configuration and insufficient samples, duration, latency or source availability
may recover automatically within the original stage deadline. The stage deadline
is exclusive: an evaluation at or after it cannot pass. The driver does not retry
reconciliation independently of the reconciler's existing retry policy.

## Observation contract

`ObservationRequest` specifies an exact publication, increasing epoch and cumulative
`since..until` window. The beginning is recorded only after matching publication
confirmation, including deduplicated unchanged state. Counts cover the whole
window with no losses; `complete = false` explicitly prevents evaluation.

Requests belong to the execution publication selected at admission and the logical
group selected inside that pinned version, including requests finishing after
publication changes. Completion-time active publication must never be used as
attribution. Count completed responses and service errors. Exclude admission
rejection and cancellation from both the numerator and denominator. The application
documents which unsuccessful responses count as failures. A reported p95 covers
accepted-to-terminal latency, including queues, over every counted completion;
report `None` when the latency population is incomplete.

Read N10 eligibility instead of recreating health tracking. Supply a semantic
`eligibility_revision` and set `eligibility_changed` if membership or eligibility
changed anywhere during the requested window, even before the first provider call.
A material change restarts the observation epoch and minimum duration without
extending the overall stage deadline. This restart requires no unchanged-weight
reconciliation. Explicit administrative resume resets both the evidence window
and overall stage deadline; pausing alone does not reset either. Stable
metrics cannot substitute for canary metrics. Configured weights allocate sticky
key buckets and do not guarantee measured exposure or effective weights after
health filtering. The integration must bound its telemetry storage; the driver
retains only the current decision and at most two group eligibility identities.

## Ownership, conflicts and lifecycle

Stage submission consumes one validated configuration snapshot: desired revision,
publication, desired state and group policies. It never rereads newer values to
replace the authorization identities during submission. The mailbox revision
comparison and publication check execute under the existing control locks before
accepting the desired update; the same publication remains its preparation guard.
A stale snapshot invalidates the unsubmitted next-stage intent. Compatible updates
restart observation of the previously applied stage before any additional traffic
can be requested, including when membership changed without changing weights. The existing worker checks that publication guard through
the atomic swap, including every retry. A superseded candidate cannot overwrite
an administrator's newer desired state or external executable publication. The
rollout preserves unrelated updates by reading the latest converged configuration
and starting a fresh observation epoch. Changed targeted weights or unresolved
groups block with a configuration conflict. All producers should use the same
`UpdateSender`; competing external publishers are detected and block progress.

`pause()` prevents additional progression and interrupts observation; a previously
requested stage may still commit. `resume()` revalidates desired state and starts
a fresh epoch, including after an observation timeout. `cancel()` synchronously
withdraws only this rollout's uncommitted pending update. An update accepted from
another producer is never withdrawn. A publication already across its atomic swap
remains active. An owned intent carries a once-only publication acknowledgement,
written under the controller lock before the mailbox freshness guard is released.
Withdrawal checks this acknowledgement under the mailbox write lock: pending
intent can be withdrawn, committed desired state remains intact, and superseded
intent cannot affect its replacement. Status reports confirmed applied weight
separately from desired weight.

Cancellation, failure and pause never restore earlier weights. Once terminal,
lifecycle methods return `RolloutError::Terminal`. Permanent or exhausted preparation/publication failures and definite condition
violations enter `Failed`; publication conflicts block for explicit intervention.
The machine rejects stale and duplicate events and cannot reactivate terminal
states. Resume is an explicit request to revalidate, not permission to overwrite
conflicting administrator policy.

The baseline publication, baseline desired revision, failed stage, applied
publication, last successful stage, terminal state and condition violation remain
in `RolloutStatus` for a future rollback policy. They retain no executable graphs.
The controller's bounded history can evict the baseline; no recovery persistence
or distributed ownership guarantee is provided.

## Decision linearization

Evidence carries an `EvaluationIdentity` containing desired revision, publication,
epoch, control generation and stage deadline. Acceptance holds the lifecycle and
mailbox guards while the controller validates the publication and accepts the
bounded state transition under its existing publication mutex. The order is
control, mailbox, controller, then rollout status. All guards are released before
tracing or application-owned cleanup. No lock spans an await, and request execution
uses no additional lock. Success, failure and final-stage completion use the same
linearization point, so stale decisions cannot become terminal rollout events.
A later configuration change can supersede a valid decision; future rollback
policy must still guard its own action against the recorded revision/publication.

## Advanced synchronization APIs

`ReconfigurationController::with_current_publication` and
`publish_if_current_guarded_with` are advanced control-plane integration primitives,
not ordinary application callbacks. They execute under the controller mutex.
Calling even `inspect()` recursively can deadlock; blocking or fallible callbacks
are prohibited. A panic in a commit acknowledgement occurs after the swap and
cannot undo the committed graph. Ordinary callers should use `inspect()` with
conditional publication, or `publish_if_current_guarded` when holding an external
freshness guard. Reassess this unconstrained callback surface before the first
public release; a constrained acknowledgement or transaction API may replace it.

## Audit and example

Structured tracing uses target `netplane_control` and events `rollout.started`,
`rollout.stage.requested`, `rollout.stage.applied`, `rollout.stage.observing`,
`rollout.stage.blocked`, `rollout.stage.passed`, `rollout.stage.failed`,
`rollout.configuration_conflict`, `rollout.paused`, `rollout.resumed`,
`rollout.cancelled`, and `rollout.completed`. Each identifies the rollout, stage,
epoch, confirmed publication and the decision or blocked reason belonging to
that transition. Event payloads are captured before a later transition changes
current status; passed records name the evaluated stage, even when advancement
has already selected the next stage. Identical blocked decisions do
not repeatedly emit polling events. Rollout IDs increase independently of desired revisions and are scoped to their
reconciler; audit records also include runtime and reconciler identifiers.

The [progressive HTTP example](../crates/netplane-http/examples/progressive_rollout/README.md)
uses real HTTP upstreams and a bounded sample provider for successful progression,
canary errors and insufficient evidence. No mandatory HTTP, Kubernetes, metrics
exporter or request instrumentation dependency was added to the control library.

## Source: docs/control-plane-observability.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# Reconciliation status and audit events

`netplane-control` exposes `Reconciler::status()` and `subscribe_status()`.
After moving a reconciler into a driver, use `UpdateSender::status()` and
`subscribe_status()` to observe the same state. The existing `driver.status()`
continues to expose typed worker outcomes and retry delays. Both channels finish
at `Stopped` after graceful completion, forced cancellation, or unused driver
drop. They are updated separately; readings taken during a transition need not
reflect the same instant. Await worker completion or drop before comparing their
terminal values. `Stopped` is terminal for a reconciler. Moving a stopped
reconciler into `ReconciliationDriver::new` creates a stopped driver with closed
update admission and both channels already reporting `Stopped`. Its `run` future
exits immediately. Submissions reject with `UpdateError::Stopped` without changing
the desired revision, failure, or status sequence; admission checks the terminal
observation inside the synchronized mailbox decision.

## Revisions and freshness

`Revision` reuses the driver's local `u64` update sequence. It identifies accepted
submissions, not an upstream resource version. Equal resubmissions receive new
revisions. Explicit `apply` assigns a revision when first polled after obtaining
the single-flight permit; a busy call does not replace the desired revision.
An unpolled call is not yet accepted. Revision exhaustion rejects new work.
Moving a previously used reconciler into a driver preserves revision numbering.

`desired_revision` identifies the latest accepted submission or invalidation, even during
coalescing or another candidate's preparation. `applied_revision` identifies the
last successful publication or equivalent-state deduplication. Coalesced or
superseded updates do not acquire fabricated applied records.
`active_publication` uses the runtime's `VersionId`, independently of revisions.
It starts with the controller's active publication and records successful
reconciliation and observed stale-token conflicts.

These are reconciliation observations. External publication and runtime shutdown
are not continuously monitored. `is_converged()` assumes exclusive publication
through this reconciler; it does not guarantee backend health or application
correctness. Use controller inspection for a separate current runtime sample.
Runtime admission counts and lifecycle remain in `RuntimeStatus`.

## Transitions and failures

Accepted input enters `Pending`, clearing its previous failure and retry count.
Validation and construction enter `Preparing`. Publication or deduplication enters
`Idle`, updates the applied revision, and clears the failure. Deduplication keeps
the publication ID. A retryable failure enters `RetryScheduled`; `retry_attempt`
counts retries scheduled after the initial attempt and saturates at `u32::MAX`.
The failure remains visible during the next preparation. Permanent or exhausted
failures enter `Blocked` until resubmission, preserving the last applied revision
and executable graph. Failure categories contain no application error strings.
The existing `ApplyError` and `DriverStatus` retain typed errors for applications.

A new submission during preparation immediately becomes the desired revision.
The older completion cannot change that revision or make it idle. Freshness checking
and publication retain the same mailbox read guard through the atomic swap. A newer
submission or invalidation can arrive after that swap and before its success event;
that successful older commit is recorded without marking newer work idle.

Invalidation advances the desired revision, enters `Blocked` with failure
`Invalidated`, and preserves the applied revision and active publication. Driver
status becomes `Invalidated(sequence)` after the prior attempt finishes. Recovery
requires a new submission. After invalidation or shutdown returns, no earlier
candidate can commit; a swap that completed first remains active.
Shutdown closes update admission immediately; `Stopped` means worker cleanup has
completed. Await the worker to confirm cleanup. Dropping an unused driver or aborting
and joining its run task also reports `Stopped`. Dropping an explicit application
future during preparation records `Blocked` with `Cancelled` and releases its
permit; subsequent explicit application can recover.

Each status value is committed atomically under a short observation lock. No lock
crosses an await. Tokio watch stores one latest value; unread notifications
coalesce and slow polling does not delay reconciliation or retain an event queue.
As with any Tokio watch API, clone the borrowed value and release the borrow
promptly; never hold a watch borrow across an await or a reconciliation call.

## Audit events

Tracing target `netplane_control` emits these typed transitions:

| Event | Level |
| --- | --- |
| `reconcile.desired_updated` | INFO |
| `reconcile.invalidated` | WARN |
| `reconcile.started` | DEBUG |
| `reconcile.applied` | INFO |
| `reconcile.unchanged` | DEBUG |
| `reconcile.superseded` | DEBUG |
| `reconcile.retry_scheduled` | WARN |
| `reconcile.failed` | WARN |
| `reconcile.stopped` | INFO |

Fields include `runtime_id` (shared with core tracing), process-local
`reconciler_id`, `event_sequence`, candidate `revision`, `desired_revision`,
`applied_revision`, `publication_id`, `retry_attempt`, and bounded `error_kind`.
`error_kind` describes the attempt identified by `revision`, independently of
`last_failure` in the status snapshot. Obsolete or post-stop failures retain their
own event category without overwriting the latest desired revision's failure.
Non-failure events carry no failure category.
Optional fields are absent when unknown. Logical event sequences increase per
reconciler, saturating at `u64::MAX`, and are also exposed in status snapshots.
Multiple reconcilers can share a runtime, so correlate sequence numbers using
`reconciler_id` rather than runtime ID alone.

Events capture the transition snapshot and emit after releasing observation,
mailbox, and controller locks. Subscriber callbacks can inspect status. Concurrent
or reentrant callbacks may deliver events out of logical order; use the sequence
rather than arrival order. A status read from a callback can already be newer
than the event snapshot. Subscriber execution is synchronous, so expensive
subscribers should offload their own work.

Events contain no configuration values, credentials, request contents, or arbitrary
upstream error text. Tracing is best-effort observability, not a guaranteed
persistent audit log. Filtering or subscriber failure can lose events. There is
no durable audit store, unbounded event queue, exporter, or administrative endpoint.

## Constructor compatibility

`Reconciler::new()` is now an ordinary function rather than a `const fn`: it
inspects the controller to initialize publication status and allocates the watch
channel. Consumers using constant initialization must construct the reconciler at
runtime. This is an intentional API change while the crate remains experimental
and unpublished.

## Source: docs/http-boundaries.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs.

# HTTP resource boundaries

`netplane-http` buffers a request body before decoding and calling `Handle::try_execute()`. Axum and Hyper parse headers before the adapter runs. The body-read semaphore is shared by clones of one adapter, uses immediate rejection when full, and does not count open sockets. The body permit is released after decoding or when collection is canceled. A request selects its graph when `try_execute()` accepts it, so publication during an upload selects the newly active graph.

| Resource | Owner | Boundary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Buffered request body | Netplane HTTP | Per-request `max_body_bytes`; `Content-Length` can reject early, streamed bodies are checked while collecting. |
| Concurrent body readers | Netplane HTTP | `max_concurrent_body_reads` counts body collection and decoding, not connections. Exhaustion immediately rejects. |
| Body collection time | Netplane HTTP | `body_read_timeout` covers asynchronous collection after headers, not header parsing or synchronous decoder CPU time. |
| Outstanding execution | Netplane core | Global admission starts after decoding and includes accepted, unfinished requests, even unpolled futures. |
| Selected graph | Netplane core | Selected at `try_execute()`, retained through accepted execution or future drop. |
| Encoded response size | Netplane HTTP | `max_response_bytes` is checked after encoding, including mapped service errors. It does not bound temporary encoder allocations. |
| Slow response writer | HTTP transport | A response can retain its bytes after Netplane admission is released. Socket writes are outside the execution budget. |
| Incomplete HTTP headers | HTTP transport | The adapter has not been called. Wire behavior is determined by Axum and Hyper. |
| Open HTTP connections | HTTP transport | No connection-count limit is supplied by the adapter. Apply server-level policy where needed. |
| Detached service work | Tower service | Dropping execution releases Netplane admission; service-owned work may continue according to that service's cancellation semantics. |

| Adapter condition | HTTP status |
| --- | --- |
| Body-read permits exhausted | 503 |
| Body too large | 413 |
| Body collection timeout | 408 |
| Failed body collection | 400 |
| Request decoder failure | 400 |
| Runtime admission exhausted or closed | 503 |
| Response encoder failure | 500 |
| Encoded response over limit | 500 |

These are adapter-level mappings. Hyper may reject malformed requests before the adapter and produce a different wire response.

`Netplane::shutdown()` closes core admission immediately and drains accepted executions. It does not cancel an upload that has not reached execution. `axum::serve(...).with_graceful_shutdown(...)` separately manages the listener and connections. The two shutdown deadlines are independent. A pending upload may finish after core shutdown and then receive 503 at admission; a stalled connection may require transport-level termination.

## Source: docs/adr/0001-tower-service-model.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0001: Tower service model

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context

Netplane needs a service composition model with readiness and request execution semantics. Tower already provides `Service` and `Layer`, and users should be able to integrate existing Tower components.

## Decision

Use `tower::Service` as the fundamental request-processing abstraction. Future graph composition must respect readiness before dispatching requests. Prototype any additional graph-specific API against ordinary Tower services before making it public.

## Consequences

Core tests can use in-memory mock services. An adapter may be needed for graph publication and version ownership, but it must preserve Tower interoperability. This decision does not choose a graph representation, public trait set, or runtime implementation.

## Source: docs/adr/0002-runtime-reconfiguration.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0002: Runtime reconfiguration

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context

Changing a running service composition must not make in-flight requests observe a partially updated graph or lose resources they still need.

## Decision

Build and validate a complete replacement graph before publication. Publish graph versions immutably. A request retains the version and resources it needs until completion or cancellation; new requests may use a newer version after publication. Define shutdown behavior alongside the first implementation. Readiness and `call()` for a request must use the same service instance and graph version, even when publication occurs between those operations. Publication must preserve resources needed by an outstanding readiness decision.

## Consequences

Tests must exercise publication during active requests and between readiness and dispatch, version isolation, and cleanup after cancellation. The publication mechanism, atomicity details, reclamation strategy, and version identifier type remain open until an in-memory prototype establishes their requirements.

The first prototype uses `ArcSwapOption` for publication. Shutdown closes admission before draining accepted futures, rejects later publication, and clears the active snapshot after draining succeeds. A timed-out drain remains retryable.

Each endpoint retains the handle for its Tower buffer worker. The worker is aborted after its last endpoint and request future owner drops, so pending readiness cannot keep an obsolete version's service alive indefinitely.

## Source: docs/adr/0003-crate-boundaries.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0003: Crate boundaries

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-14

## Context
