Transport dependencies can constrain reuse and make graph behavior harder to test. The workspace currently contains one library crate and `xtask`.

## Decision

Keep graph composition and execution in `crates/netplane`, independent of concrete transports and deployment systems. `xtask` remains development-only. Add another crate only when a real dependency or public API boundary is demonstrated. A future transport adapter may depend on the core; the core must not depend on the adapter.

## Consequences

Core behavior should be testable with mock Tower services and no sockets. Hyper, Kubernetes, and deployment integrations are deferred. The decision does not prohibit optional features or later crates when a prototype justifies them.

## Source: docs/adr/0004-graph-composition.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0004: Internal graph composition prototype

**Status:** Accepted for the internal prototype

**Date:** 2026-10-17

## Context

Tower readiness has no request argument. A router that selects a backend from the request cannot promise that backend's readiness in its own `poll_ready`. Netplane already owns bounded endpoints, immutable publication, and global admission. The integration prototype composes these pieces without adding a public graph API.

## Decision

Use typed, acyclic Tower composition for sequential middleware and one selected branch per request. The example and integration test use a `FilterLayer` before an internal request-aware router. The router owns cloneable `Endpoint` handles for two named, independently owned backend services. It chooses synchronously from `&Request`, then transfers the request to exactly one endpoint. Cloning a handle does not clone the raw service.

The selected endpoint's worker polls readiness and calls its own service instance. Each backend has explicit concurrency and buffer capacities. The complete root is validated through `GraphDraft` and published as one immutable version. Accepted requests retain their selected version; endpoint execution futures retain worker ownership. An unmatched route must be rejected explicitly unless a fallback was deliberately configured. The two-branch prototype has an exhaustive parity route.

At the prototype stage, this model did not define a graph schema or public graph construction API. Cycles, fan-out and joins, mutable nodes, shared service instances, and serialized declarations remained outside the decision.

## PR 10 extension

`GraphBuilder` makes the prototype's single-router topology public. It validates named service targets, route labels, the explicit fallback, entry, reachability, and capacities before creating endpoint workers. Middleware remains ordinary Tower composition on registered services. Each compiled version carries deterministic metadata describing declarations and capacities. The builder does not support nested routers, cycles, fan-out, joins, or policy verification. `GraphDraft` remains the direct single-root API.

## Readiness alternatives

Per-backend buffering is the prototype choice. It lets each endpoint own readiness and dispatch, works with stateful non-`Clone` services, and isolates an unready A worker from B. It adds one worker and bounded queue per backend. The router may itself report readiness while the selected endpoint is saturated; backpressure then appears as a pending execution future. `RuntimeLimits::max_outstanding` bounds accepted callers, including unpolled futures and callers waiting at either queue.

Direct readiness-aware routing might reduce queues and worker overhead, but the route is unknown during the router's `poll_ready`. Selecting after readiness would require synchronization or reservations that preserve the same service instance and version, with possible head-of-line blocking. These are design considerations, not measured performance or complexity results: the prototype implements only per-backend buffering.

The outer graph endpoint also has a concurrency limit. A waiting A request consumes one outer execution slot, so that limit must leave capacity for B to progress. If all outer slots are occupied by A, B can wait even though B is ready. The integration test demonstrates B progress with one A request and two outer slots; it does not claim isolation under arbitrary A saturation.

## Ownership and cancellation

Netplane guarantees its accepted-request budget is released when an execution future completes or is dropped. It retains selected versions and endpoint worker references for accepted requests, and aborts a worker after its last Netplane owner disappears. Queued waits can be canceled. A dispatched call's cancellation behavior, any work spawned by a service, and the duration of that work belong to the user-supplied Tower service. Shutdown closes admission immediately and waits for accepted futures to drain; it cannot force a service's independent work to stop.

## Findings and follow-up

The prototype tests demonstrate that `call` follows successful backend readiness, B completes before A becomes ready when an outer slot is available, and a non-`Clone` stateful service works through its endpoint. Publication lets old work complete on old backend instances, and obsolete workers release after their last owners disappear. Backend errors propagate without rerouting. The configured Tower buffer supplies the queue bound; the prototype's dispatch test asserts the concurrency limit rather than measuring queue occupancy. Independent backend readiness does not guarantee independent progress when all outer slots are occupied. These findings informed the public `GraphBuilder` extension above. Application policy validation remains outside its scope.

## Source: docs/adr/0005-reconfiguration-control.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0005: Reconfiguration control

**Status:** Accepted

**Date:** 2026-10-17

## Context

Applications need concurrent administrative callers to replace and inspect a running graph, and sometimes restore a prior validated executable graph. A graph object is not a publication generation. Tower services cannot generally be reconstructed or cloned.

## Decision

`ReconfigurationController` exclusively owns one `Netplane` publisher. A short-lived mutex serializes control operations; execution handles continue to select versions through the existing atomic active store. Callers capture a snapshot and its runtime-scoped `VersionToken`, validate candidate graphs outside the lock, and submit both for publication. Foreign and stale tokens fail without a swap or automatic retry. The controller uses the same publication primitive as direct `Netplane::publish()`.

Published wrappers share an `Arc<GraphVersion>`. A rollback takes the executable graph from retained history and publishes a new wrapper with a fresh generation. It therefore preserves Tower service state, readiness ownership, and request lifetimes. Controller history retains at most the configured number of displaced publications in publication order. A zero limit disables rollback. In-flight requests may keep evicted versions alive.

Shutdown closes admission while holding the control mutex, clears history, and returns the runtime's drain future. A timeout remains retryable, but rollback history is never restored. Inspection reads active ID, graph metadata, and the matching token from the same loaded publication. Controller publication and shutdown events are emitted after releasing the control mutex so subscriber callbacks may inspect the controller.

## Reconciliation invalidation

The optional control driver checks its input mailbox under a read guard and passes
that guard to `publish_if_current_guarded`. The controller drops it after the atomic
swap and controller unlock, before tracing callbacks and displaced-version cleanup.
Producers serialize submission, invalidation and shutdown through the mailbox write
lock. Thus an earlier candidate cannot commit after invalidation returns; a swap
that completed first remains active. The order is mailbox then controller, with no
lock held across preparation awaits. Core remains independent of reconciliation
schemas and discovery systems.

`with_current_publication` accepts bounded control-plane decisions under the
existing controller lock without publishing. `publish_if_current_guarded_with`
acknowledges successful swaps under that lock and before releasing the external
freshness guard. These callbacks must only update internal synchronization state:
no blocking, reentry, tracing or application callbacks. Both operations preserve
the existing mailbox-before-controller lock order and add no request-path lock.

## Consequences

Control callers must inspect after conflicts and decide whether their candidate still applies. A historical publication may be evicted even while request futures still use it. `version.released` describes publication wrapper ownership, not necessarily final executable graph reclamation. Persistent history, health decisions, transport administration, and graph diffing remain outside this API.

## Source: docs/adr/0006-backend-health.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0006: Backend health outside immutable graph publication

**Status:** Accepted

## Context

Discovery membership does not establish operational availability. Rebuilding a
graph for each failed request would entangle live observations with desired-state
reconciliation and reset service ownership unnecessarily.

## Decision

Compose transport-independent health handles with existing routing policies and
ordinary Tower layers. Registries retain weak records keyed by endpoint incarnation;
graphs, observations and probe registrations own strong handles. Backend-local state
transitions invalidate observation generations. Passive recovery admits traffic
after cooldown; active recovery requires successful active probes before eligibility.
Observation tokens distinguish passive calls from probes. Duplicate probe registrations
share ownership only with a matching configuration identity; changes are rejected
while an old registration is retained. Registration capacity covers the union of
active, historical, in-flight, and candidate backend identities.
A shared caller-owned scheduler bounds registrations and simultaneous checks.
Fallible graph selectors return a typed error when no positive eligible weight
remains. Health never changes immutable graph membership or an issued destination.

## Consequences

Health survives compatible publication and rollback through handle ownership.
Known replacement identities start fresh. Transport and discovery dependencies stay
outside core. Health decisions sample backend-local eligibility; they are not a
global transaction. Passive recovery allows ordinary configured traffic and is not
a full circuit breaker. Eligibility can redistribute all traffic to a remaining
canary, so future rollout control must account for effective traffic weights.

The contract and lifecycle are described in [backend health](../architecture/health.md).

## Source: docs/adr/0007-progressive-rollouts.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from docs/adr.

# ADR 0007: Guarded progressive traffic rollouts

**Status:** Accepted

## Context

Gradual canary traffic needs explicit evidence attributed to a published version
and logical backend group. Runtime-wide counters cannot establish that exposure
occurred. Configuration reconciliation already owns bounded construction, desired
revision invalidation and optimistic publication.

## Decision

Keep rollout policy inside optional `netplane-control`. An immutable specification,
pure condition evaluator and deterministic machine authorize desired weight
changes. A caller-owned driver submits them to the existing reconciler using a
mailbox revision comparison and a publication guard retained through every retry
and the atomic swap. A single validated snapshot binds next-stage submission to
its observed revision and publication; rejection discards that authorization and
reobserves the previous stage. Eligibility-triggered resets preserve the polling
cadence, including when reconciliation interrupts a wait. No new executable
publisher or request-path mechanism exists.
At most one rollout owns a reconciler. Observation and control use bounded latest
snapshots, one outstanding provider future and finite deadlines. Evidence resets
preserve the original stage deadline; only explicit resume may reset it. The first
stage cannot reduce exposure below the applied baseline.

Applications resolve groups, preserve unrelated configuration and provide complete
publication-attributed evidence with authoritative N10 eligibility identities.
Missing evidence blocks; the final stage requires successful evaluation. Material
membership or eligibility changes invalidate the window. Exact integer basis
points avoid floating point error-rate decisions.

## Consequences

Commit acknowledgement is written under the controller lock while the mailbox
freshness guard still excludes withdrawal. Cancellation withdraws only owned
pending intent; it preserves committed desired state and cannot undo traffic.
Evaluation acceptance holds lifecycle and mailbox guards and validates publication
under that same controller mutex. Thus final success and definite failure have an
explicit linearization point, independent of event delivery. Timeout and lost
ownership remain halted until explicit resume, regardless of subsequent updates.
Pause may allow an already requested publication to finish. Failure does not roll
back. Status retains identifiers and decisions for N12 without retaining executable
graphs or promising history retention. Integrations own telemetry, source freshness,
response classification, shutdown coordination and endpoint membership identities.
See the [rollout contract](../progressive-rollouts.md).

## Source: QUICKSTART.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from ..

# Quick start

HTTP example: `cargo run -p netplane-http --example reconfigure`. Start `curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/a` in another terminal; it waits on v1. Press Enter in the example terminal to publish v2. A second `curl http://127.0.0.1:3000/a` returns v2 while the first still waits. Press Enter again to release the v1 request, then Ctrl-C to stop the listener and drain Netplane.

Netplane is a Rust library workspace. Its library crate provides bounded Tower service endpoints, atomic publication of immutable execution versions, and bounded graceful draining.

## Prerequisites

- Rust via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/); `rust-toolchain.toml` selects 1.88 with rustfmt and Clippy.
- Git for cloning the repository.
- Optional: `cargo-nextest` and the tools used by the full quality gate script.

## Build and verify

```bash
git clone https://github.com/janagor/netplane.git
cd netplane
cargo metadata --no-deps
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo build --workspace
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo bench -p netplane --no-run
```

`cargo test --workspace` includes documentation tests. If `cargo-nextest` is installed, use `cargo nextest run --workspace` for the test suite. Run `./scripts/quality-gates.sh` for the repository's broader local checks; it may require additional tools reported by the script.

Nix users can enter `nix develop`, then run the same Cargo commands. Toolchain consistency between the Nix shell and `rust-toolchain.toml` is part of the separate environment and CI work.

## Where to work

- `crates/netplane`: public library code with bounded execution, version publication, and shutdown admission.
- `crates/netplane-http`: optional HTTP adapter, not a core runtime dependency.
- `crates/xtask`: repository automation, not a runtime dependency.
- `docs/architecture.md` and `docs/adr/`: design contract and decisions.
- `AGENTS.md`: coding and review instructions.

Read [the architecture](docs/architecture.md) before changing graph types or adding transport adapters. Add a dependency only with its first consumer. Keep the core independent of sockets, Hyper, Kubernetes, and specific deployment environments.

`GraphDraft::validate()` checks capacity settings and prepares an endpoint with a Tower buffer worker, so call it inside a Tokio runtime. `Netplane::publish()` swaps the active version atomically while running; requests already selected keep their previous version. `Netplane::shutdown(grace_period)` closes admission when called and returns a future that waits for accepted request futures to finish or be dropped. Successful draining releases the active graph, including when handles remain. A timeout leaves admission closed and can be retried; publication remains closed during and after shutdown.

`GraphBuilder` validates one router with named backend services, declared route labels, an explicit fallback, and positive endpoint capacities. It does not support arbitrary DAGs, nested graphs, or dynamic node editing. `ReconfigurationController` adds token-checked publication and bounded rollback history over validated versions.

Run the in-memory transition example with `cargo run -p netplane --example live_reconfiguration`. It changes a direct Backend A service into a router with a simulated authorization filter for Backends A and B while an old request is in progress, then drains accepted work during shutdown. See [execution semantics](docs/architecture/execution-semantics.md) for the guarantees and limits.

## Source: SECURITY.md

> Relative links in this section resolve from ..

# Security Policy

## Supported Versions

Netplane is currently an unpublished Rust library. Security fixes are applied to
the `main` branch.

| Version | Supported |
| ------- | --------- |
| latest `main` | ✅ |
| older snapshots | ❌ |

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Do not open a public GitHub issue for security vulnerabilities.**

Report vulnerabilities by opening a
[GitHub Security Advisory](https://github.com/janagor/netplane/security/advisories/new).

Please include:

- A description of the vulnerability
- Steps to reproduce
- Potential impact
- Suggested fix (if any)

The maintainer will respond through the private advisory channel.

## Rust-Specific Security Practices

Netplane uses the following security practices:

### Dependency Auditing

```bash
# Check advisories, licenses, banned crates, and sources
cargo deny check
```

This check runs on pull requests and pushes to `main`.

### Supply Chain Security

- `deny.toml` configures `cargo-deny` with:
  - Allowed licenses list
  - Banned crates list
  - Advisory database checks
- Dependabot is configured to propose dependency updates weekly

### Unsafe Code

- The library forbids unsafe code.

### Secrets and Credentials

- Never commit secrets, tokens, API keys, or credentials
- Use environment variables or secret management systems
- The `privacy-first` skill in `.agents/skills/privacy-first/` enforces no email
  addresses in the codebase

Repository security settings, including Dependabot alerts and branch protection,
are managed on GitHub and are separate from the checks defined in this repository.
